# 17-expanse — sources

P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Researchers (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Priyanka Raghunathan → [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work"; the fine-tuning run is the author's.
- Tobias Brandt → [HN] the genomics comment (bursty pipeline, "about 8 different steps", "We need to reserve the $MAX requirements for each").
- Ana Lucía Ferreira → [HN] the student's "so I overestimate" on simulation time; the queue wait for a big request is the author's.
- Kwabena Owusu → author's invention, filling a gap: an ML engineer whose sizes come from past runs on a dashboard, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance and Current solution).
- Mei-Ling Zhou → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story at a quant fund, GUESSED by code.
- Rafael Moreno → author's invention: a vague, habitual story (GUESSED), echoing [HN] "everyone over-requests by two to three times".
- Ingrid Haugen → author's invention: a gate No (writing up, no jobs that week).
- Samuel Adeyemi → author's invention: a gate No (away at a conference).
- Yusuf Demir → [HN] "snooping on sumbit scripts ... many of them are egregiously bad": a copied script holding eight GPUs.
- Claire Dubois-Martin → author's invention, filling a gap: a licensed binary with no source code, so the tested condition fails ('no').
- Hiroshi Takeda → [HN] "at least for everyone else, I'd would prefer tuning my own usage myself": he profiles a test run (Current solution mostly works; Adoption friction no).
- Fatima Al-Sayed → [HN] "you lose days of work"; the walltime limit and the group allocation are the author's.
- Diego Castañeda → [HN] the student's PDE simulation ("If I'm running a PDE simulation, and I allocate n machines I want to use all of them"); he keeps his margin (Adoption friction probably not).

Cluster operators (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).
- Beatrix Okoro → [HN] "What you are really left with is the 'small and medium business' clusters that are purpose specific": a small cluster, less waste, a lower rung.
- Thomas Reinholt → [HN] the security objection ("a hard no"); would not pay.
- Leilani Kahale → [HN] "In many places the cost of the HPC hardware isn't passed onto them": a grant-funded university cluster that does not measure the waste (dont_know) and has no line for a monthly fee.

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

screens.why1: Right after I said how researchers size jobs today, checking how that sizing turned out is the obvious next screen.
screens.why2: Two of the five rows are cut off mid-sentence ('The job ran, but we asked', 'the request was a poor'), so no researcher or I can read what they mean even on a second pass.
screens.why3: Every researcher knows whether their last job ran clean, sat on idle GPUs or died mid-run and had to be resubmitted.
screens.why4: Rows 2 and 3 are truncated nonsense, so the common true answer (it ran but held far more GPUs or memory than it used) has no readable option, and nothing separates a little padding from a lot.
screens.why5: My rungs about padding and idle reserved compute come out garbled. The box's bar names 'The job ran, but we asked' while Keel's own bar names 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle', which is not on the list, so the screen no longer says what I typed.
screens.why7: The first rung works and the last fails outright, but the rung just above the line is an unreadable fragment, so the line may not sit under a working rung. The two bars disagree, one naming a rung not on the final list. Rungs 2 and 3 do not say how the job turned out on the one measure of wasted or lost compute.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How did the sizes you requested turn out? -- It ran to the end, using about what I asked · Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle · ┄ line ┄ · It ran, but most of what I reserved sat idle · It failed mid-run and I had to resubmit · It never ran to the end at all · I can't recall

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs just before the study goes out, after the problem steps are checked.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the option I picked, "Lock and record the face Keel preselects", made me read it twice to see that it means keeping the AI interviewer's default face.
screens.why3: It's my own study and my own call how researchers get interviewed, so I can answer it from what I know.
screens.why4: The choices cover AI versus me, but "lock and record the face" is product-speak rather than words I'd use, and it doesn't plainly say I can pick another face or record myself.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed about Expanse is rephrased here, and no product or role detail leaks to the researchers.
screens.instead: Who should ask researchers your questions? — Keel's AI interviewer, with the face Keel picked / Keel's AI interviewer, with a face I choose / Me, recorded on video

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, deciding how my researchers will answer is the obvious next step before the link goes out.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, and let them choose are plain to me, and I can tell at once which suits researchers who live in terminals and Slack.
screens.why3: I know my researchers well: they would rather read and click through a short form between job submissions than sit on a video call with an AI, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options cover AI video, text only and both, and each one is distinct; 'tap' is a phone word for people at a workstation, but the meaning is clear.
screens.why5: It keeps my segment wording, 'researchers and ML engineers', and nothing about Expanse or the cluster operators leaks into the choice.

screens.why1: After choosing how researchers answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending the study out.
screens.why2: Three plain options; "open link" and "signs in with Google" are everyday words to anyone who runs a research or infra team.
screens.why3: I know whether I'm sending to named researchers I've met at HPC centres and labs, or posting in a SLURM users channel, so this is answerable from my own outreach.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover it, but the second option's "Contacts page" refers to a screen I haven't seen in this flow, so it needs a second read.
screens.why5: No product or role words leak, and my pick (each person by name) is kept as typed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (one link each) / People from a Keel contact search (one link each, I send them) / A group, one open link I post where they already are (e.g. a cluster users' Slack or mailing list)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside 'Frequency: 4 counted', but the 5 needed to call it is only on the card below, and it does not say why Frequency is named when Importance and Current solution also stand at 4 counted.
screens.why_b2: The tally reads at once: 4 beliefs, 1 holding and 3 too few, over 7 people, and each card shows its count against its bar (6 of 7 at a bar of 6 of 7; 4 counted of 5 needed).
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my lines word for word, but Prevalence and Frequency are framed as a job failing mid-run, which is the risk that makes everyone over-request rather than the guessing and waste I described.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the screen never says to get one more counted researcher per card, or what the held Prevalence means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible everywhere, the three thin cards are called too few rather than leaned on, and Prevalence at exactly its bar is marked 'at the bar' rather than strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: three beliefs have 4 of the 5 counted answers they need (3 of the 7 were not counted), so get one more counted researcher each; failures mid-run were near universal (6 of 7).

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar", so I know my belief held and that it held with no room to spare.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 6 cells for and 1 against on a 0-to-7 axis, with the marker at 6 labelled "at least 8 in 10", so what is counted, over how many, and where my bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the failure mid-run from my own words, but the belief drops my segment's qualifier "on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs", and the Asked line's tag "the most recent time it happened" doesn't fit a yes/no gate.
screens.why_b4: The So line notes I'm exactly at the bar and points to the next two cards, but it never says that one more No would flip this or what that means for building around failed runs.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and nothing calls a result exactly at the bar strong.
screens.instead: Holding at your bar exactly: 6 of 7 researchers on 100+ GPU SLURM/K8s clusters had a job fail mid-run this week; one more No and it wouldn't hold, so treat it as a lean and widen the sample before betting on failure-prevention as the lead.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly above '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip and the median at 4 read quickly, but the axis starts at 0 when no one can answer 0, and the legend's 'what you said' versus 'at what you said' takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: My belief is about guessing memory, GPUs and walltime at every submission; 'have a job fail mid-run' is the result of under-guessing, not the act itself, and the question carries a stray '— the most recent time it happened', so I recognise the topic but not my claim.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not say that one more counted answer at 3 or above settles it, or what I should do in the meantime.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted, why two were dropped), the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing is claimed beyond the four.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 4 of 4 counted say a job failed mid-run on 3 or more of the last 5 working days (middle answer 4); one more answer at 3 or above settles it, so send to one more researcher, and ask about the guess at submission rather than the failure.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, 4 counted and 5 needed, so I know where I stand and why.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes plain what is counted (8 picks from 4 people), and the bars add up, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' sits next to '4 counted', so I had to look twice to see which 4 is the bar and which is the people.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Importance, the belief line is word for word the one I checked, and my own item is on the list as 'the problem you named'.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me that 3 of my 4 already put it in their two, or that one more counted researcher would settle it, or whom to send it to.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the two uncounted people are named with their reasons, and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call' with no claim beyond 4 people.
screens.instead: 3 of 4 put guessing memory, GPUs and run time in their two, and Kwabena, whose sizes come from past runs, did not. One more counted researcher decides it, so send it to a few more who size jobs by hand.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits directly over its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the two agree.
screens.why_b2: The per-rung counts and the line are clear at once, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a ghost cell next to only 4 counted takes a second look before I see it means 4 of 5 people once the floor is met.
screens.why_b3: The belief line and the bar's rung, 'Padded it a little; it ran, a little idle', are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't say that 3 of my 4 counted already fell short, or that one more counted answer is what I need.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing is claimed beyond the four counted.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 counted fell short (2 doubled everything, 1 job died and was resubmitted), one short of the 5 needed, so get one or two more researchers to answer before you lean on it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know the answer and why at once.
screens.why_b3: The box is named Importance and the belief line is word for word the one I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed' implies I need one more researcher to answer, but the screen never says so. It also doesn't say what Kwabena's rival pains (data movement, software setup) mean for my pitch, or why Current solution has no box here.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the low count is named as too few to call, and the single quote is tagged as the one against rather than presented as a trend.
screens.why_b6: Kwabena's line adds something I didn't type: researchers whose sizes come from last week's runs lose their day to moving data onto nodes and getting libraries to agree. Those are the pains competing with sizing.
screens.instead: Importance: too few to call (4 of 5 needed). Get one more researcher's answer; the one against sizes from past runs and loses the day to data movement and library setup, so check whether that rival pain is common.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it plainly checks whether I am on the kind of shared cluster the study is about, before anything else is asked.
screens.why2: Cluster and GPUs are my everyday words, but I would have to stop and think whether 100 or more GPUs means the whole cluster or what my jobs can reach, since our cluster has more cards than any one job I submit.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our shared SLURM cluster is, so I can answer from what I see every day.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it for a size gate, and no escape is right for a screener.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's segment of researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters has lost the word shared and the scheduler, so a big private box could also pass.
screens.why6: It is short, one question, and yes or no is easy to hold when heard.
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes cluster with 100 or more GPUs in total? Yes; or No.

screens.why1: Right after the screener confirms I'm on a 100-plus GPU cluster, asking whether a job of mine died partway through in the last week is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "A job fail mid-run" is exactly how I'd say it to a labmate; nothing to reread.
screens.why3: I know whether any of my jobs died in the last five working days; I check squeue and my logs every day.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it and don't overlap; the chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: The founder's problem is a job killed because memory, GPUs or time were under-requested, but "fail mid-run" also takes in my own bugs, NaN losses and node crashes, so the condition that made it the problem has dropped out.
screens.why6: One short question with the window up front, then "Yes or no", which I can answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: The measure and shape are right (two fixed answers, no escape, and a No is truly possible), but the gate has drifted from the founder's problem to any mid-run failure, so Yes will be inflated by failures that have nothing to do with the resource guess (the card's dropped-condition pitfall).
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did a job get killed mid-run for going over its memory or time? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes to having a job fail mid-run this week, asking how many of those five days it happened on is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: 'Job fail mid-run' and 'working days' are exactly how I'd say it about my SLURM jobs, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I see every failure in my job logs or squeue history, so I can count the days from what I actually saw this week.
screens.why4: One button per day from 1 to 5 covers every true answer after my yes, none overlap, and 'I can't recall' is the right way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'fail mid-run' takes in node crashes and my own bugs, not just jobs killed for under-requesting memory, GPUs or time, so it drifts a little from guessing resources up front.
screens.why6: It is one short sentence, then 'a number from 1 to 5' and the escape, which I can hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Every option counts days in the window, the buttons run 1 to the window's count of 5 with no 0 and no bands, the unit is said once, the escape is there and is the only one, and a founder's low of 2 or more would split the buttons.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did you have a job killed mid-run for running out of memory or time? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After two screens on jobs failing mid-run, asking which part of a run on the cluster I'd most like made easier is an obvious next step.
screens.why2: Allocation, memory, GPUs, run time, moving data, waiting in the queue and getting software working are all everyday words on a shared SLURM cluster, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: These are the things I deal with every time I submit, so I can pick from what happened on my own last runs.
screens.why4: The rows are distinct and the set is close to complete, but *Running out of the group's allocation* is a bad outcome, not a task, so it reads oddly after *made easier* next to the four *-ing* chores.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product reaches me, and *guessing memory, GPUs and run time* is how I would describe the job-script step myself.
screens.why6: One short question with five short options spoken as a list and one escape; the three-part guessing row still says easily.
screens.why7: The own item is there, not first, with four rivals, *None of these* at the first ask, and the belief can go either way, but the allocation row breaks the card's rule against bad outcomes as rows, and the own row is a three-item list that only restates the circumstance.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of jobs on the cluster. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Staying within the group's allocation · Guessing memory, GPUs and run time · Moving data on and off the cluster · Waiting for a job to start · Getting software working on the cluster · None of these

screens.why1: After asking how often my jobs died mid-run, asking how my last guess at memory, GPUs and run time went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Sizing memory, GPUs and wall time, padding the request, and a job dying and being resubmitted are exactly how I talk about my own jobs.
screens.why3: I size and submit my own jobs, so I know how the last one went.
screens.why4: 'Copied an old script and hoped' is a method with no outcome, and it overlaps the others: my copied script could also have run as planned or died; there's also no rung for 'sized it from past runs and it still OOMed'.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or the founder's plan reaches me, and 'I can't recall' fits a job I sized myself.
screens.why6: Spoken, each option is two clauses run together ('padded it a little, it ran, a little idle'), which is a mouthful to hold five times.
screens.why7: There is a working first rung, so the belief can go either way, but the rungs mix methods with outcomes, mix two costs (idle waste against death), and the last rung is a method rather than the job failing outright.
screens.instead: Think of your last job. How did what you asked for in memory, GPUs and run time turn out? About right, it ran as planned · A bit too much, some sat idle · Far too much, much sat idle · Too little, it died and I resubmitted · Too little, it died and I gave up -- or I can't recall.
